data.title: 'I'm burned out': I'm constantly helping my cousin who is running out of money. Is it too much to expect his sister to help?
data.description:
By Quentin Fottrell

'I spend a lot of time away from my family and spend money on gas, taking him out to eat'

"He co-owns several acres of property with his sister." (Photo subject is a model.)

Dear Quentin,

I'm trying so hard to find my cousin a suitable/nice senior living place to live. He has no income and has come to the end of the money his parents left him, 15 years ago, to live on. He is physically fine, but has had trouble managing his life.

He co-owns several acres of property with his sister (who has plenty of money and who inherited most of their parents' sizable estate). She lives in a different state, which makes it much harder for her to help with his everyday needs.

She has helped a lot, but things weren't done in a timely way - that is, not anticipating his needs before he went on Medicare. He is no longer thriving living alone in a small cabin on the acreage they co-own.

It's almost too much work for me, even, but it would be much easier if he could have access to the money that equals his half of the acreage they co-own. Then he could move to the very good place (that I've found for him) until he "spends down" his money.

Then he would go on Medicaid and live in a studio apartment at the same good place I have found for him, which is not too far from where I live. I'd be close enough to drive to visit him and help him with things when needed.

She is behind the 8 ball, as usual, moving too slowly, and talks about moving him way too far away from me to be able to visit him very often. All of this should have been thought about long before now, but I wasn't privy to a lot of things.

Sadly, she wants her brother cared for, but seems to want to rely on me to do everything I can without paying for things needed - only things that she thinks are necessary. It takes me well over an hour to get to his place now, and I'm getting burned out.

I don't know how best to help without having my own immediate family suffer because of all the time I'm away and the money I spend on gas, taking him out to eat, etc. What can I do?

The Cousin

Related: 'I'm not interested in long-term care insurance': I'd like to retire at 55. How much will I have to pay for healthcare?

You can email The Moneyist with any financial and ethical questions at qfottrell@marketwatch.com. The Moneyist regrets he cannot reply to questions individually.

Your cousin's sister may have a vested interest in your cousin not selling this property or going to a Medicaid-approved nursing home.

Dear Cousin,

You know the old saying: There are no victims, only volunteers.

You have willingly decided to help your cousin navigate his retirement years, spend time with him by taking him for lunches/dinners and put a plan in place for him so he can live comfortably without running out of money.

At the same time, you have resentments towards his sister who you believe - rightly or wrongly - that she should pitch in and help. You believe she is reneging on her duties to her sibling, and wonder why she doesn't do more.

So I have two pieces of feedback for you here: first, if you do continue to pitch in with your cousin, do so without rancor. Spend only the amount of time with him, and money on gas, as you are comfortable with and as you can afford to.

These boundaries are yours to build. Your cousin will gladly accept the company and assistance you give him, but if you're doing this while quietly cursing his absent sister or your credit-card bill, don't do it, or show up only as much as you can.

It may be that your cousin's sister has her own interests at heart, too. Because she is a co-owner of the property, her financial interests and your cousin's aren't necessarily aligned. They very likely have different priorities and goals.

If your cousin were to die without a will, she could inherit his interest in the property. In other words, she may have a vested interest in her brother not selling this property or making other decisions that could affect the value of her potential inheritance.

Your cousin needs help, from a CFP or financial adviser or, better yet, free legal aid. In particular, I would want an elder-law attorney who practices in the state where your cousin lives to look at the property ownership, finances and government benefits.

Understanding Medicaid rules

The other issue: You feel a moral duty and responsibility towards your cousin, and genuinely want to help him. You can feel burned out and resentful, and also love your cousin and want him to be secure and happy. Both things can be true.

For what it's worth, Medicaid treats a person's primary residence as an exempt asset when determining eligibility for many Medicaid programs, although the rules vary significantly by state. Ask an elder-law attorney to review the circumstances.

As of January 2028, Medicaid programs will only cover expenses for long-term services and supports (LTSS) if the recipient's home equity does not exceed $1 million. There is an exception to that new limitation for homes located on agricultural property.

Co-owning this property with his sister does not in itself prevent Medicaid eligibility. However, selling, gifting, or in any way "spending down" your cousin's share of the property needs to be handled carefully, as that could come back to bite you later.

A transfer for less than fair market value could potentially result in a Medicaid penalty under the five-year look-back rules. Selling the property for fair market value would also give your cousin funds, which would be included if determining his eligibility.

Medicaid estate recovery rules would also allow the state to seek reimbursement for certain long-term-care expenses after your cousin's death. Depending on the state law, this could result in a claim against his ownership interest in the property.

Your cousin, I presume, has some Social Security, however modest. Social Security retirement benefits and Social Security Disability Insurance count as income for Medicaid eligibility, even if parts of that money are non-taxable.

You'll be able to help him better when you have all the facts.

data.title: 'My total balance should be $20 million': I invested $1.1 million in a crypto platform. Have I lost it all?
data.description:
By Quentin Fottrell

'I invested on the recommendation of an executive vice president of a major New York investment bank'

"My personal banker believes the individuals involved are scammers." (Photo subject is a model.)

Dear Quentin,

I invested in a cryptocurrency-trading exchange on the recommendation of an executive vice president of a major New York investment bank. Although I believe the VP and this foreign crypto platform are real, my personal banker believes the individuals involved are scammers.

The following is a summary of my interactions concerning this investment scheme:

-- My banker contends that everyone involved in this investment is fake and is a scammer - my friend, the adviser, and the people at the crypto platform. The adviser I used is an executive VP at a major New York investment firm.

-- She repeatedly warned me not to tell anyone because she could be heavily fined and imprisoned for violating FINRA and her company's financial laws. I have not investigated or contacted FINRA because I don't want my recovery amount to be jeopardized.

-- The adviser controlled and dictated every action I took while trading on the platform from May 20 through June 30. All communication between the adviser and me was conducted through WhatsApp.

-- The adviser made every decision. She told me how to withdraw the money and transfer it to my bank account, how to make the wire transfers, and what to say to my bank. She also solely communicated directly with the cryptocurrency broker.

-- My initial investments totaled $1.1 million. As of June 30, my total assets were $2 million. Based on the return on investment that my adviser guaranteed, my total balance should be $20 million by the end of August.

I contacted the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center to investigate, but they determined that I had not provided them with enough information. Whenever legal professionals hear that the investment involves a foreign market, they decline to work with me.

Do you know of, or can you suggest, what recourse I have to recover these funds? If the U.S. adviser is real and is working as an executive VP for a New York investment bank, how can I get someone to investigate this case? Or have I lost it all?

Crypto investor

Related: I lost $240,000 after a 'friend' I met on Instagram encouraged me to invest in crypto. Can I write off my loss?

You can email The Moneyist with any financial and ethical questions at qfottrell@marketwatch.com. The Moneyist regrets he cannot reply to questions individually.

Scams are financial and psychological. You don't want to blow the whistle on this VP because you believe that will jeopardize your "investment."

Dear Investor,

No real investment opportunity is a sure thing.

I removed the name of the crypto platform and your personal bank, but I did some cursory research on the platform in question. There are discussion boards over 7 months old that allege the platform is indeed a scam, and furthermore say that the numbers you see on your screen are likely fictitious, whether they're $2 million or $20 million.

Your investment balance is the financial equivalent of communicating with a potential romantic partner, and believing that their photo is real, even though nothing else makes sense about what they have told you; the photo, of course, is probably AI or taken from another dating profile. The same is very likely true for your magically inflated crypto balance.

First off, that discussion board was very likely online before you appear to have made your initial investments. Secondly, always beware of anyone who promises you a guaranteed return on investment. There's no such thing, and should set off a huge alarm bell. Thirdly, legitimate investment advisers and wealth managers don't conduct business over WhatsApp.

The numbers you see on your screen are likely fictitious, whether they're $2 million or $20 million.

I honestly don't know whether this executive VP is an unwitting victim who has been persuaded to invest their own cash, or whether they are an agent of the alleged scammer. If investigated, whatever the truth, they would presumably claim to be the former. Going forward, however, take the FBI's advice: give them every last detail and document and individual.

Scams are both financial and psychological. You don't want to blow the whistle on this VP because you believe that will jeopardize your investment. But there was very likely no "investment" to begin with and, given that she is based in the U.S. and gave you all the instructions, they would likely be a person of interest in this case and even a gateway to the larger organization.

Such confidence schemes are known as "pig butchering" - a particularly rancid term for a rancid business. Scam artists scour social-media platforms, public records, country clubs, social events, and dating sites. They then take their sweet time "fattening up" their marks, cultivating trust and gradually feeding them promises of bigger and better returns.

The Financial Industry Regulatory Authority (FINRA) does investigate crypto scams, but only if they involve FINRA-registered brokers, brokerage firms or crypto assets that qualify as securities. The FBI will investigate if the alleged scam involves U.S. citizens and U.S. wire services. But you need to accept that your money may be lost, and proceed with full disclosure.

Related: My father coerced me into giving $100K to a 'lucrative' cryptocurrency pyramid scheme. I'm suspicious about how it works

FBI warnings

The FBI warns investors about the methods scammers use to huckster successful, smart people. Chief among the carrots is the promise of seemingly irresistible returns. They often find their victims through social media, text messages, dating sites, messaging apps such as WhatsApp and Telegram, online advertisements, or even third parties, the bureau says.

When contact is established, scammers work to build trust through flattery, shared personal experiences, romantic interest, fake testimonials and, yes, promises of love or money, the bureau adds. They may initially allow small withdrawals to make the investment appear legitimate and provide step-by-step guidance on making larger deposits.

Once the victim is hooked, the scammer advises the investor to open a crypto account at a reputable exchange, transfer money from a traditional bank account to the new cryptocurrency account, convert the money to the crypto and, finally, open an account on the "investment platform" provided by the scammer or an individual. This is your story almost to the word.

Once the victim is hooked, the scammer finally convinces victims to open an account on the "investment platform."

There has been success in tracking down stolen/scammed funds. The Justice Department said in July 2025 that it took legal action against the operators of a fraudulent cryptocurrency investment platform. According to the FBI, scammers contacted victims through social media and lured them with promises of high returns and little risk.

The platform displayed fake profits to encourage additional investments, then demanded fraudulent fees or taxes when victims tried to withdraw their funds. One victim in Missouri reportedly lost more than $16 million, while millions of dollars in suspected scam proceeds were allegedly laundered through cryptocurrency.

Go back to the FBI and tell them everything you know. Spare no detail and no individual who you believe was involved in this scheme. Keeping your executive VP on your good side won't help you now, and trying to negotiate with the crypto platform and/or WhatsApp contacts will only flummox you further and attempt to deter you from taking action.

The FBI handles international cyber frauds and cross-border financial crimes. As it did with that case from July 2025, the bureau uses blockchain analysis and partners with international law enforcement agencies to track overseas cybercriminals, freeze accounts, dismantle large-scale fraud rings and, hopefully, return some or all of the money to the victims.

Once again, however, there are no guarantees.

data.title: Par Health Issues Voluntary Nationwide Recall of Two Lots of Dexmedetomidine HCl in 0.9% Sodium Chloride Injection Due to the Presence of Particulate Matter
data.description:
Par Health Issues Voluntary Nationwide Recall of Two Lots of Dexmedetomidine HCl in 0.9% Sodium Chloride Injection Due to the Presence of Particulate Matter

Par Health Issues Voluntary Nationwide Recall of Two Lots of Dexmedetomidine HCl in 0.9% Sodium Chloride Injection Due to the Presence of Particulate Matter

PR Newswire

ROCHESTER, Mich., Sept. 18, 2026

ROCHESTER, Mich., Sept. 18, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Par Health is voluntarily recalling two lots of Dexmedetomidine HCl in 0.9% Sodium Chloride Injection 400 mcg/100 mL (4 mcg/mL) to the hospital level. The product is being recalled due to the presence of particulate matter identified as cellulose or stopper material. 

Administration of Dexmedetomidine HCl in 0.9% Sodium Chloride Injection 400 mcg/100 mL, found to contain particulate matter, has a reasonable probability of causing life-threatening adverse health consequences including pulmonary emboli (blockage in pulmonary blood vessels), occlusions of other blood vessels (which can lead to tissue death and possible organ damage), and/or inflammation of the walls of veins, which may lead to clotting. To date, Par Health has not received any reports of adverse events related to this recall.

Dexmedetomidine HCl in 0.9% Sodium Chloride Injection 400 mcg/100 mL (4 mcg/mL) is formulated for intravenous infusion. The product is indicated for sedation of initially intubated and mechanically ventilated adult patients during treatment in an intensive care setting and for sedation of non-intubated adult patients prior to and/or during surgical and other procedures.

Recalled product can be identified as follows and by vial label images included with this release:

Product Description

NDC

Lot

Expiration Date

Dexmedetomidine HCl in 0.9% Sodium Chloride Injection 400 mcg/100 mL (4 mcg/mL) for Intravenous Infusion, Distributed by: Par Pharmaceutical

42023-187-01

88802

04/2027

These lots were distributed nationwide to wholesalers between May 13, 2025 and June 29, 2025.

Par Health is providing written notification to wholesale accounts that have received the affected lots and are arranging for return of all existing inventory of Lots 87558 and 88802 through Inmar, Inc. Wholesale distributors and hospital pharmacies that have the product being recalled should immediately discontinue use and stop distribution. If you have further distributed the recalled product, please notify your accounts or any additional locations which may have received the recalled product.

Questions regarding this recall can be directed to Inmar, Inc. at 1-833-599-3197 Monday through Friday between the hours of 9 a.m. and 5 p.m. ET or by email at rxrecalls@inmar.com.

For medical or technical product information or to report a product complaint or adverse event please call 1-800-828-9393 Monday through Thursday between the hours of 9 a.m. and 8 p.m.  ET or Friday between 9 a.m. and 6 p.m. ET.  

Adverse reactions or quality problems experienced with the use of this product may be reported to the FDA's MedWatch Adverse Event Reporting program either online, by regular mail or by fax.

  • Complete and submit the report Online: www.fda.gov/medwatch/report.htm 
  • Regular Mail or Fax: Download form www.fda.gov/MedWatch/getforms.htm or call 1-800-332-1088 to request a reporting form, then complete and return to the address on the pre-addressed form, or submit by fax to 1-800-FDA-0178

This recall is being conducted with the knowledge of the U.S. Food and Drug Administration.

data.title: Robbins LLP Urges BBNX Stockholders Who Lost Money Investing in Beta Bionics, Inc. to Contact the Firm for Information About Leading the Class Action
data.description:
Robbins LLP Urges BBNX Stockholders Who Lost Money Investing in Beta Bionics, Inc. to Contact the Firm for Information About Leading the Class Action

Shareholder rights law firm Robbins LLP reminds investors that a class action was filed on behalf of all persons and entities who purchased or otherwise acquired Beta Bionics, Inc. (NASDAQ: BBNX) common stock between July 30, 2025 and February 24, 2026, inclusive (the "Class Period"). Beta Bionics is a commercial-stage medical device company that offers an automated insulin delivery system for the treatment of diabetes, known as the iLet Bionic Pancreas insulin pump (“iLet”).

The complaint alleges that defendants misled investors regarding the viability and efficacy of iLet.

Investors who suffered significant losses during the Class Period may be eligible to participate in the lawsuit and should contact Robbins LLP for information before the November 3, 2026, lead plaintiff deadline.

Listen to our podcast.

Why Was Beta Bionics Sued?

The complaint alleges that during the Class Period defendants touted the safety, efficacy, and commercial success of iLet—the Company’s sole commercialized device. In October 2025, Beta Bionics disclosed that it had received an FDA Form 483 raising concerns about iLet. Defendants stressed that the letter had nothing to do with the safety or efficacy of the device itself. Rather, defendants stated that the FDA had only taken issue with the Company’s interpretation of which customer complaints needed to be reported to the FDA, such that the Company would have to backfile some additional customer complaints that were very minor in nature and required no medical intervention. Further, defendants assured investors that the Company was swiftly implementing the FDA’s required changes to its complaint reporting system, and accordingly that they did not “foresee any ongoing challenge with this at all.”

Plaintiff alleges that defendants’ statements were materially false and misleading. The FDA had in fact raised numerous serious issues with the iLet device itself, namely that the device was malfunctioning and dosing patients with dangerously high levels of insulin, causing hypoglycemic events. Thus, the complaints numbered in the thousands and included hundreds of life-threatening events requiring significant medical intervention. Additionally, the Company had utterly failed to implement any meaningful corrective actions.

Why Did BBNX Stock Drop?

A series of disclosures beginning on January 8, 2026, and concluding on February 24, 2026, revealed that the issues raised in the warning letter went far beyond mere complaint handling.

On February 24, 2026, the full truth was revealed when the FDA publicly released its warning letter detailing a litany of violations and defendants’ failure to correct them, and contradicting months of defendants’ public statements that all back-filed complaints were for entirely benign issues. The warning letter made clear that defendants’ prior interpretation of FDA reporting requirements had not been reasonable and had excluded numerous serious patient incidents that clearly should have been reported.

The stock, which was trading at $31.99 per share on January 9, 2026, fell to $12.89 per share by February 25, 2026.

What Is a Lead Plaintiff?

The lead plaintiff is a court-appointed investor who represents the interests of all class members throughout the litigation. Shareholders who wish to lead the case should contact Robbins LLP before the November 3, 2026, lead plaintiff deadline.

Serving as lead plaintiff is not required to share in any potential recovery. Investors who do not seek appointment may remain absent class members if the case proceeds and later resolves successfully.

Does It Cost Anything to Participate?

No. Robbins LLP represents investors on a contingency fee basis.

Why Robbins LLP?

A recognized leader in shareholder rights litigation, Robbins LLP represents investors in securities fraud and shareholder derivative litigation. We have helped restore more than $2 billion in value to shareholders and secured some of the largest recoveries in shareholder derivative litigation history.

"Companies have an obligation to provide investors with complete and accurate information so that markets can function fairly and efficiently," said Brian J. Robbins, Founding Partner of Robbins LLP.

To be notified if a class action against Beta Bionics, Inc. settles or to receive free alerts when corporate executives engage in wrongdoing, sign up for Stock Watch today.

Contact Robbins LLP

Investors seeking additional information about the Beta Bionics, Inc. securities class action may contact Robbins LLP by submitting an inquiry, emailing attorney Aaron Dumas, Jr., or calling (800) 350-6003.

data.title: Building Bridges for the Right to Worship Act
data.description:
Building Bridges for the Right to Worship Act

Building Bridges for the Right to Worship Act

PR Newswire

LAS VEGAS, Sept. 18, 2026

CoHNA's Las Vegas chapter hosted an interfaith event with policymakers
to back the bipartisan legislation even as CoHNA spoke in support of the bill on Capitol Hill

LAS VEGAS, Sept. 18, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- The Las Vegas chapter of the Coalition of Hindus of North America (CoHNA) hosted a community gathering in support of the Right to Worship Act on September 16, 2026, at the Sahara West Library, in Las Vegas. The bipartisan bicameral bill seeks to protect worshippers from intimidation and disruption via a 100-foot, protest-free buffer zone around houses of worship during religious services. Peaceful expression protected by the First Amendment is excluded from the bill's prohibited activities. 

The event was held under CoHNA's Building Bridges and Connecting Communities initiative, which brings faith and civic leaders together around shared concerns and values. It was one of two CoHNA coast-to-coast engagements on the bill that day. As the Las Vegas chapter convened local leaders in Nevada, CoHNA leadership was also in Washington, DC, making the case for the same legislation at the press conference, organized on Capitol Hill, by its Congressional sponsors.

In Vegas, the afternoon opened with an introduction to CoHNA and its government affairs work, followed by a short presentation on the Right to Worship Act, by CoHNA's director of government relations Sudha Jaganathan.

Several policymakers and Congressional staff attended the event. Among them was Nevada Assemblywoman Heidi Kasama who spoke to the interfaith community. We were also pleased to have with us Senator Catherine Cortez Masto's Las Vegas staff assistant Martin Hernandez as well as Senator Jacky Rosen's Las Vegas regional director Nethmini Happawana.

Speakers from across Las Vegas's religious and civic landscape also offered brief remarks. Vin Manjing, a nun with the Nevada Buddhist Association, said that religious communities need to come together, be strong, and protect their faith

B. Bhatti from the Gurdwara Guru Nanak Parkash spoke on behalf of the Sikh community. He highlighted that Sikhism teaches respect for all people and for human values, and reiterated that religious freedom matters for everyone. 

Byron Brooks, representing the Jewish Federation and StandWithUS of Nevada, described a climate in which bad actors have been emboldened and conditions have grown progressively worse for most faith-based organizations, including Jewish Americans, who have faced a sharp rise in antisemitism since October 7.

Speaking for members of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, Corey Wozniak called the bill a wise measure and said that as a religious person he felt protected by it.

Farrah Acheson of the Nevada Muslim Caucus spoke to the rise in Islamophobic attacks alongside other forms of religious hostility. She urged minority communities to come together and make clear that they are an integral part of America and are not going anywhere. She pointed to her own Jewish and Hindu friendships as evidence of what united communities can accomplish.

Pushpita Prasad, CoHNA's chief communications officer, spoke for the Hindu and Jain communities. The Las Vegas Hindu-Jain Temple and the Fiji temple were represented at the gathering as well.

José Melendrez, vice provost at University of Nevada, Las Vegas, addressed the university's role in community engagement. Students from diverse communities share the campus, he noted, and the divisions that came to the forefront nationally after October 7 required sustained effort at UNLV to keep the peace through a period of heated exchange. Everyone has the right to speak up, he reiterated, which is precisely why finding peaceful ways to work together is critical.

Swadeep Nigam of VegasDesi, a community news portal, who helped convene many of the day's guests, also spoke at the event.

The range of voices in the room mirrored the coalition behind the bill nationally: more than 30 national organizations have endorsed the Right to Worship Act, among them the Anti-Defamation League, the Islamic Society of North America, United Sikhs, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops, the National Association of Evangelicals, the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, and CoHNA.

Each of the three Southern Nevada Congressional members and the two Senators in DC have acknowledged the Right to Worship Act and are reviewing these; and when it comes to vote, the Las Vegas community hopes they will stand to protect the American Right to Religious Freedom and the Right to Worship without intimidation or curbing any congregant or devotee from their places of worship.

"Nevada showed today that protecting places of worship is not an issue for any one faith," Jaganathan said. "Multiple faith communities came together to endorse a simple principle: we should be able to worship freely and without fear, and that does not weaken the right to peaceful expression," she added. 

Capitol Hill Support

Across the country, in D.C. the same day, CoHNA's chief operating officer and New Jersey chapter director Hitesh Trivedi joined a press conference held by Rep. Tom Suozzi (D-NY) and Rep. Brad Knott (R-NC), the bill's House co-leads, alongside representatives of more than a dozen national religious organizations, urging both chambers to advance the legislation this Congress. A Senate companion measure has been introduced by Sens. Ted Cruz (R-TX) and Elissa Slotkin (D-MI).

Trivedi spoke about the dozen Hindu temples that have been desecrated, vandalised, or threatened, and in one case even shot at, since 2022. He said these incidents of Hinduphobia send a chilling message to the broader Hindu community. The bill, he said, would help ensure that "devotees of every faith can visit their places of worship and pray without fear, amid a time of rising Hinduphobia."

About CoHNA
CoHNA is a grassroots level advocacy and civil rights organization dedicated to improving the understanding of Hinduism in North America by working on matters related to the Hindu community and by educating the public about Hindu heritage and tradition. For more information, please visit https://cohna.org or follow us on Twitter, Facebook, LinkedIn and on Instagram.

data.title: Lockheed Martin Gets $871 Million Navy Contract for Work on Jet Sites
data.description:
By Katherine Hamilton 




  Lockheed Martin received an $871.2 million contract from the Navy to fund continued work on sites for fighter jets. 



  The amount is an add-on to a previous contract to provide additional capacity for support equipment under the F-35 Lightning II site activation and hardware non-recurring sustainment effort. 



  The contract provides initial sustainment supplies and services in support of establishing and activating land-based and at-sea operation sites for F-35 jets. 



  The sites are for the Air Force, Marine Corps, Navy and foreign military sales customers. 



  About 90% of the work will be done in El Segundo, Calif., with the other 10% happening in Fort Worth, Texas. It is expected to be completed in February 2031.

data.title: Utilities Down as Treasury Yields Test Multiyear Highs — Utilities Roundup
data.description:
Shares of power producers fell as Treasury yields tested multiyear highs.

The yield on the two-year Treasury note closed at the highest level since July 2024. Yields on 10-year and 30-year Treasurys closed on the brink of 19-year highs.

The utilities sector has been under pressure because it is exposed to bond yield changes on multiple fronts.

The SPDR Select Utilities exchange-traded fund, which tracks the utilities industry group of the S&P 500, fell by almost 1.4% Friday and is now down roughly 5% for the year to date.
